name: MCP3002-I_SN
title: MCP3002: 2.7 V, two-channel, 10-bit SAR A/D converter with SPI interface
summary: A 10-bit successive-approximation converter with a built-in track-and-hold and a two-input multiplexer. The two inputs work either as two single-ended channels measured against VSS or as one pseudo-differential pair, chosen by the command word that starts each conversion. The supply pin is also the reference, so full scale equals VDD, anywhere from 2.7 V to 5.5 V. It talks over an SPI-compatible port (modes 0,0 and 1,1) and converts at up to 200 ksps at 5 V or 75 ksps at 2.7 V; raising CS puts it in standby, where it draws a few nanoamps.
key_figures: 200 ksps max at VDD = 5V; 75 ksps max at VDD = 2.7V
525 µA typ, 650 µA max at 5 V
SPI, modes 0,0 and 1,1; fCLK up to 3.2 MHz at 5 V

notes: The code reads device, temperature range, then package: MCP3002 or MCP3002T (tape and reel, offered in SOIC and TSSOP only), I for industrial, then MS, P, SN or ST.

pins.name: CS/SHDN
pins.function: Chip select and shutdown. Driving it low starts a transfer; driving it high ends any conversion and drops the part into low-power standby. It has to return high between conversions.

pins.name: CH0
pins.function: Analog input, channel 0. Single-ended input of its own, or one half (IN+ or IN-) of the pseudo-differential pair.

pins.name: CH1
pins.function: Analog input, channel 1. Single-ended input of its own, or one half (IN+ or IN-) of the pseudo-differential pair.

pins.name: DIN
pins.function: Serial data in: the start bit and the channel-configuration bits are shifted in on it.

pins.name: DOUT
pins.function: Serial data out: the conversion result leaves on it, one bit per falling clock edge while the conversion runs.

pins.name: CLK
pins.function: SPI clock. Clocking starts the conversion and moves each result bit out; a minimum clock rate applies (see Minimum clock rate).

pins.name: VDD/VREF
pins.function: Supply, +2.7 V to 5.5 V, and the converter's reference input.

circuits.title: Two-pole active anti-aliasing filter driving CH0
circuits.description: An MCP601 op amp wired as a two-pole low-pass (Sallen-Key) stage with gain feeds CH0 from a low output impedance and removes signal above the band before it can alias. R1 and R2 in series with C1 fed back from the output and C2 to ground set the poles; R4 and R3 set the gain. CH1, the IN- input, is tied to ground with VSS. VDD, which is also the reference, is bypassed by 10 µF and 1 µF to ground. The serial lines go to the host.

equations.name: Clock rate limit for holding the sample

operation.text: A SAR converter. The input is tracked on the internal sample capacitor for 1.5 clock periods, beginning on the second rising clock edge that follows the start bit; then the input switch opens and the held charge is converted, one bit per clock, into the 10-bit result.

The command word before each conversion picks the input arrangement: two single-ended inputs measured against VSS, or one pseudo-differential pair with CH0 and CH1 assigned as IN+ and IN-. IN+ may swing from IN- up to IN- plus VDD; IN- must stay within ±100 mV of VSS. IN- lets small common-mode noise riding on both inputs cancel out.

operation.topic: Codes near the rails in pseudo-differential mode
operation.text: With IN- more than 1 LSB below VSS, IN+ must go below VSS before 000h appears; with IN- more than 1 LSB above VSS, 3FFh needs IN+ above VDD.

The 20 pF sample capacitor has to settle to 10-bit accuracy within the 1.5-clock sample time. Source resistance RS sits in series with the internal switch resistance and slows that charging, which worsens the offset, gain and INL. A near-zero source impedance is best, such as an op amp like the MCP601, whose closed-loop output impedance is tens of ohms. The graph of maximum clock frequency against input resistance gives the clock that keeps INL within 0.1 LSB of nominal for a given RS.

Each input pad (CHx) carries 7 pF of pin capacitance (CPIN), ESD diodes to VDD and VSS with a 0.6 V threshold (VT), and ±1 nA of junction leakage. Behind it a sampling switch with 1 kΩ of resistance connects the 20 pF sample-and-hold capacitance (the DAC capacitance) to VSS. RSS in this model is the signal source's own impedance.

Pull CS low to begin. If power came up with CS already low, CS must be taken high and low again first. The first clock edge that sees CS low and DIN high is the start bit. Leading zeros on DIN before it are ignored, so a host can pad the command to whole bytes.

After the start bit come SGL/DIFF (1 = single-ended, 0 = pseudo-differential), ODD/SIGN (the channel in single-ended mode, the polarity in pseudo-differential mode) and MSBF. Sampling runs from the second rising edge after the start bit to the third clock's falling edge.

DOUT is high-impedance until the falling edge of the MSBF clock, when it gives a low null bit. The next 10 falling edges give B9 down to B0. Data always changes on falling clock edges. With MSBF = 1, further clocks with CS low give zeros. With MSBF = 0, the word is sent again LSB first (B1 to B9 following B0) before zeros follow.
CS may go high at any point to end the conversion. Taking only the top 8 bits and starting the next cycle at once raises the conversion rate.

Once the result has been shifted out (tDATA), the bias circuit and comparator power down and the reference input becomes high-impedance, and CLK can carry on, shifting out the LSB-first word or zeros.

An MCU SPI port set to shift out on the falling edge and sample on the rising edge works in mode 0,0 (clock idles low) or 1,1 (clock idles high). Send two bytes: the first is 0, 1 (start), SGL/DIFF, ODD/SIGN, MSBF and three don't-care bits; the second is all don't-care. B9 appears on DOUT as clock 6 falls. The first received byte then ends with the null bit, B9 and B8, and the second holds B7 to B0.

Charge bleeds off the sample capacitor while a slow conversion runs. At 85°C the held charge stays good for 700 µs at VDD = 2.7V and 1.5 ms at VDD = 5V, so the 1.5 sample clocks and 10 conversion clocks must fit inside that time; otherwise linearity falls outside the ratings. At 70°C and above, fCLK must be at least 10 kHz.

A source that is not low-impedance needs a buffer, or results will be inaccurate. A low-pass filter ahead of the input keeps out-of-band signals from aliasing into the results; an op amp stage can buffer, filter and add gain at once.

A bypass capacitor, 1 µF recommended, belongs on this part in every design, placed as close to the VDD pin as possible. Keep digital and analog traces apart, run no traces under the converter or its bypass capacitor, and keep fast lines such as the clock well away from analog traces. Use an analog ground plane so all parts share one ground potential, and feed VDD to each device in a star from one point to avoid shared return-current errors.
